claims.text: Standard W–Cu fabrication methods such as spark-plasma sintering can produce interfacial voids.
Standard W–Cu fabrication methods can produce phase separation.
Ultrafast pulsed laser treatment of tungsten surfaces before copper infiltration can create a nanostructured W–Cu alloyed interfacial layer.
Ultrafast pulsed laser treatment locally melts the tungsten surface.
The laser-induced interfacial layer improves copper wetting.
The laser-induced interfacial layer promotes metallurgical bonding between tungsten and copper.
Tungsten has a melting point of approximately 3422 °C.
Processing under an inert atmosphere is required for the proposed treatment.
The laser treatment and copper infiltration can be performed while keeping processing temperatures below tungsten's melting point and below conditions of rapid copper vaporization.
A nanostructured W–Cu interfacial alloy layer minimizes void nucleation.
W–Cu phase boundaries impede thermal transport.
Rapid solidification following laser-induced localized melting creates a thin W–Cu interfacial alloy.
The thin W–Cu interfacial alloy reduces interfacial surface energy.
Improved copper wetting suppresses void formation and phase separation during infiltration.
Relative to spark-plasma-sintered W–Cu, laser-treated W–Cu will have a lower void fraction.
Relative to spark-plasma-sintered W–Cu, laser-treated W–Cu will have more uniform interfacial bonding.
Relative to spark-plasma-sintered W–Cu, laser-treated W–Cu will have higher thermal conductivity.
Relative to spark-plasma-sintered W–Cu, laser-treated W–Cu will retain equivalent or better mechanical durability under fusion-relevant heat and irradiation.
Mechanical alloying can produce W–Cu composites with void formation and phase separation.
The long-term stability of the laser-induced interfacial alloy under sustained irradiation and thermal cycling is unknown.

contradictions.description: The intervention and mechanism require localized melting of tungsten, which implies that the affected surface reaches at least the tungsten melting temperature, while the conditions and boundary state that processing temperature must remain below tungsten's melting point. A distinction between bulk temperature and transient local surface temperature is not specified.

The initial state is described as tungsten particles or a skeleton already within a copper matrix, but the intervention is specified as occurring before copper infiltration. The proposed process sequence and the source of copper needed to create a W–Cu alloy before infiltration are therefore internally unclear.
